title: Personal data; birthplace at Nora; family home
description: Charlene Olson begins the interview with the personal data record. Ella Lillian Olson says she was born November 18, 1897, in the tiny settlement of Nora four miles from Troy, which once had a store, blacksmith shop, barber shop, post office, and saloon. All nine children were born in the family house, which has since been torn down.

title: Mother's and father's origins; siblings and their deaths
description: Ella tells how her mother, Lena Granley, was born near the Swedish border in Norway and came to America at six, settling in Minnesota before homesteading near Troy, and lived to nearly 99 in a nursing home. Her father, Oly Oster, was born in Värmland, Sweden, and died in 1923. She names her eight siblings and explains how the brothers died young, including a heart attack, a ruptured appendix, a loading accident in Coos Bay, and suicide, leaving only three sisters.

title: Husband Walford; courtship and marriage; his work
description: Ella describes her husband Walford, born in Dassel, Minnesota, and their marriage on November 13, 1920, under an arch of Oregon grape and cedar boughs in the house where she was born. He worked as a logger and later managed the Latah County Grain Growers warehouse until his legs gave out. He died three years earlier, after 52 years of marriage.

title: Schooling; work in Spokane; logging camp and cook wagon cooking
description: Ella went through ninth grade, working for her room and board in Moscow, then went with a friend to Spokane to find housework, earning $29 a month. Back in Idaho she cooked for crews and became head cook in the Troy Lumber Company logging camps and mill. She courted Walford through his World War I service and cooked on a harvest cook wagon in the Genesee country, baking bread while the wagon moved and shoveling mud from the floors during the rainy 1920 season.

title: Decision to marry; children; grandchildren
description: Ella says she married at nearly 23 because she was tired of working, and had two sons, Reinnle and Marvin, born at home with a doctor, whereas her mother had a neighbor woman instead of a doctor for all nine births. Marvin recently survived a severe car wreck in Lewiston. She names her grandchildren and great-grandchildren, and explains that she raised grandson Terry after his mother died of diabetes.

title: Facts of life; childbirth; family size
description: Ella says her generation's mothers never discussed pregnancy or the facts of life, so young people learned on their own, though she did see a doctor during her pregnancies. She had only two boys despite wanting a girl, knew of no birth control, and recalls the large families of eleven or twelve children common in her mother's time. Her granddaughter Beverly Lorraine was given the girl's name she had picked out for her son.

title: Hobbies; baking; Troy's history in photographs
description: Ella mentions crocheting, needlework, gardening, and baking all her own bread, though she never entered fairs. Looking at old photographs, she recalls the town being called Bulmer—mispronounced by the many Swedes—before becoming Troy, when Main Street in 1891 was full of stumps amid wild woods, and she comments on how farmland and new building have since changed it.

title: Church life; Dorcas Society; sports and community events
description: Ella was baptized in the Swedish Methodist church, confirmed in the Nora Mission Church built the week she was born, and later attended Lutheran and Nazarene churches before joining the Adventist Church in 1954, where she led the Dorcas Society for years. Her sons went to Lutheran Sunday school. She recalls never missing Troy basketball tournaments and attending one football game before deciding the sport was too rough.

title: Depression years; relief; housing
description: During the Depression Ella's family lived in a rented house in Troy while her husband could find no work, surviving on a town sewer project that rationed hours and on government food relief. Their wealthy bachelor landlord let the six-dollar monthly rent slide, and they stayed in that house for ten years.

title: Depression-era jobs; hospital laundry work
description: Ella Lillian Olson describes her husband's public works jobs in town and her own work washing and ironing at Dr. Myers's hospital, which was packed with patients from townships around the area. She worked there until the Myers family left for Seattle, and her household later rented and bought the Arnist house.

title: Son's war service; Depression hardships
description: She tells of her son Raynold's four years in World War II around Guadalcanal and Hawaii, and explains why she considers the Depression, with its uncertainty about food and clothing, the worst time of all.

title: Pea-picking trips; mica cutting; retirement pastimes; throat surgery
description: She recalls carpooling to night-shift pea-picking near Moscow, including a freezing breakdown and a car accident, then cutting mica at the local plant until 1954. In retirement she enjoyed gardening, baking, embroidery, and quilting until throat surgery in Spokane forced her to stop.

title: Small town life; childhood play; Swedish language; country school
description: She praises small-town safety and friendliness, remembers building playhouses in the woods, and describes starting school at five speaking only Swedish. Her father donated land for the new Pleasant Hill schoolhouse, and an older schoolmate once tricked her into circling a stump through recess.

title: Strict teachers; school discipline
description: She describes young, overwhelmed teachers and the harsh punishments of Mr. Steelsmith, who kicked boys' legs apart and jabbed pupils' hands over penmanship. She contrasts this with Mrs. Butte, a kind teacher from Avon who kept control without meanness.

title: Television and reading; generational change
description: She mentions watching As the World Turns and reading church papers, then reflects on her granddaughter's rustic life in the Montana woods and how machinery and scarce jobs have changed young people's prospects while education has improved.

title: Marriage roles; courtship at logging camp; wartime letters
description: She describes making most decisions in her marriage because her quiet husband was helpless in old age, and her fear of dying first. She recounts meeting Wofford while cooking at a logging camp, his letters from the war, and their leap-year marriage in 1920.

title: Advice on small towns; bank robbery; views on work and working mothers
description: She advises young families to choose small towns for children's safety, recalling the local bank robbery. She voices her belief in the value of work, criticizes mothers who leave babies with sitters, and reflects on child discipline past and present.

title: Oldest child burdens; family size; sewing and canning
description: She describes the heavy chores and blame she bore as the oldest child, baking bread and tending the barn from age seven. She discusses her mother's large family, smaller modern families, and her own lifelong sewing contrasted with younger working women who lack time for canning.

title: Family recreation; antique sales; widowhood; sister's family
description: She recalls Model T outings and overnight huckleberry-picking trips, trading the car for a radio, and selling a wood stove and glassware at a recent antique sale. She touches on living alone in widowhood with her wedding keepsakes and on her sister's six sons and their schooling, service, and marriages.

title: Wartime photograph; son at Rosario store
description: Charlene Olsson and Ella Lillian Olson look at photographs, including one of Olson's son taken during the war by the water canal. Olson identifies another son who works at the Rosario store and whose looks have not changed, and a picture of her mother that appeared in the paper.

title: Expectations of marriage; deciding family size
description: Olsson asks what girls expected from marriage, and Olson recalls assuming she would have a house full of children even though she did not want many. Having cared for her younger brothers at home, she had not wanted boys, but had two sons and decided that was enough.
